doc.title: Frank Tiberi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 30, 2022

title: Benny Goodman and repairing horns
summary: Tiberi played with Goodman, who called him Cheech, and fixed horns for Benny Carter, Gerry Mulligan, Al Cohn and Charles Lloyd.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: You mentioned that you are looking at a lot of notes to yourself.
For this interview and I wonder if there’s something I haven’t asked about that you’d like to —
Well I was with Benny Goodman.

And of course he called me “Cheech.” And if he called you by your nickname then he liked you. I mean there were a lot of players with me: Kenny Burrell, Ruby Braff, Doc Severinsen. And of course we went on the road with Urbie Green. These were some of the things actually. But another thing actually was I was a good repairman too. Benny Carter, every time we did the Norwegian he would always call me into his room and I had to change a pad you know. And this happened twice. And oh Gerry Mulligan had a gig of a concert and we were following him in New York and one of the players said the post on his horn broke, on the baritone, he couldn’t play. And one of the players said, “Frank is coming in” because he knew me you know he played with our band and he said, “When he comes in he’ll fix it.” I did. I grabbed it and I soldered the post and he played.
That’s a great way to be in good with other musicians. Save their horns.

I did. I fixed Al Cohn’s horn also as well. And actually let’s see, up in — my note over here it seems like I remember — oh the reason why I went with Benny Goodman was Wardell Gray you know. He liked the way —

And so I played maybe like him at that time actually. I was sort of like Zoot and Al and that’s the reason why I got called. A friend, a photographer named Bootsie told Benny that you’ve got to hear this guy or something like this, and I got the gig. But what’s his name Charles Lloyd, I’m in Pompeii, Italy and we had a night off over there and I get a
knock on the door and it’s Charles Lloyd and his B key was hanging. And he says, “Frank, I’ve got a gig tonight.” And you know, “Can you do something for me?” I fixed his horn too.
I think it’s a wonderful connection that you heard Benny Goodman which made you take an off ramp from the classical world into jazz and then you got to play with him.
Yeah that’s right. Yeah. There are some exciting moments also.
Was he as absent minded as many of those stories indicate?

Well you know at that stage of the game I think he was a little old then, he wasn’t just as great as he was actually. But I mean it was only like the concert that we had around — it was an outside concert with the group, with a small group, we had a couple of concerts with the small group and the band also. But after that he didn’t really attend too much. It was Urbie Green that took the band out on the road, with the Benny Goodman band.
